title: Metrics & Time-Series Data
summary: What makes a metric useful in practice, the data model underneath tools like Prometheus, and why averages lie.

slides.markdown:
Every metric is one of three shapes, and picking the wrong one makes a metric useless.

| Type | What it measures | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Counter | A value that only ever increases (until reset) | Total requests served |
| Gauge | A value that goes up or down | Current memory usage, active connections |
| Histogram | A distribution of observed values, bucketed | Request latency (lets you compute percentiles) |

**How to decide:** if it can go down, it's a gauge, not a counter — using a counter for something that decreases (like queue depth) breaks every rate calculation built on it.

Prometheus (and most modern metrics systems) identify a metric by **name plus labels** — `http_requests_total{method="GET", status="200", service="checkout"}` is a distinct time series from the same metric name with `status="500"`. Labels let you slice one metric name along multiple dimensions without defining a separate metric for every combination.

This is powerful, but every unique label *combination* creates a new stored time series — which is exactly the cardinality trap covered a few Cards from now.

Metrics reach the backend one of two ways.

| Model | How it works | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Push | Each service actively sends metrics to a collector | Works well for short-lived jobs; collector must handle inbound load from everyone |
| Pull | The backend scrapes each service's `/metrics` endpoint on an interval | Backend controls its own load; requires every target to be discoverable and reachable |

**How to decide:** pull (Prometheus's model) fits long-running services well since the backend paces itself; push fits ephemeral or batch jobs that might not exist when a scrape would happen.

slides.sectionTitle: Cardinality can take down your monitoring
slides.markdown:
**Cardinality** is the number of unique label-value combinations for a metric. Adding a label with an unbounded value — a raw user ID, a full request path with dynamic segments, a UUID — multiplies the number of stored time series, sometimes by millions, turning a cheap metric into one that exhausts the monitoring backend's memory or blows past its cost budget.

The fix is discipline at instrumentation time: label values must come from a small, known set (status codes, method names, service names) — never anything with effectively unbounded cardinality.

An **average** collapses a distribution into one number: 99 requests at 10ms and 1 at 10 seconds averages to about 110ms — hiding that one user had a terrible experience. **Percentiles** report where a fraction of requests land: p50 is the median, p95/p99 show what the slow tail experiences.

Interview framing: p99 matters because a platform serving millions of requests has millions of users hitting that tail daily — not a rare edge case at scale, a guaranteed daily occurrence for someone.

slides.sectionTitle: A healthy p50 while p99 is on fire
slides.markdown:
Worked example: a dashboard shows p50 latency steady at 40ms — looks fine. But p99 has crept from 200ms to 4 seconds over the same window. The average barely moved because only a small fraction of requests are affected, but that fraction is real users, and it's growing.

Digging in, the p99 requests all hit a specific cache-miss path that's degrading as cache eviction increases under load — invisible in p50 because most requests still hit cache. Watching only p50 (or a plain average) would have missed this entirely until it got much worse.
